explanations.explanation: The narrow door, baker. Jesus says, “Make every effort to enter through the narrow door.” Someone asked Him for a number, and I think He handed back something to DO instead. That's one answer a calculator can't help with.

Close, because it does sound like the kind of thing a person would want. But in Luke 13:24 Jesus doesn't say wide and He doesn't say gate. His words are “the narrow door.” It's a short passage, so one word can hide a lot.

The Beautiful Gate is a real place, a temple gate where a man who was lame from birth was set down every day to beg (Acts 3:2). But it isn't in this passage. Here Jesus says to make every effort to enter through “the narrow door.” Nice name, wrong building.

I get why this one tempts you, because trying hard feels like it should always work. But Jesus says, “For many, I tell you, will try to enter and will not be able.” So the text says many will try and not be able. That's why He says to make every effort.
Right, baker. Jesus says, “For many, I tell you, will try to enter and will not be able.” So trying isn't the same as getting through. That's why He tells them to make every effort.

explanations.answer: I do not know where you are from
explanations.explanation: That's it. Once the door is shut and the knocking starts, the master of the house replies, “I do not know where you are from.” There's no morning appointment and no waiting room in what Jesus says. Just that one line, and then they get ready with their reasons.

explanations.answer: Come back again in the morning
explanations.explanation: I like a good second chance, but that's not what the master says. Jesus says he replies, “I do not know where you are from.” Nothing in the passage mentions morning. Tomorrow is not in that sentence.

explanations.answer: Wait there until I call for you
explanations.explanation: That would be a patient master, but it isn't the text. The master answers the knocking with, “I do not know where you are from.” He says it, and in verse 27 He says it again. No waiting list is mentioned.
Evildoers is the word, baker. The master says, “Depart from me, all you evildoers.” It's a heavy line, and I'm not going to joke on it. The knocking in verse 25 ends with this answer.

Hypocrites is a word that fits in other places, but it isn't the one here. In verse 27 the master says, “Depart from me, all you evildoers.” It's a serious moment, so the exact word matters. The word on the card is evildoers.
That's a word that sounds right in a sermon, but it's not what the master says. His words are, “Depart from me, all you evildoers.” It's a heavy moment in the passage. Jesus' word is evildoers.

explanations.answer: Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets
explanations.explanation: Yes! Jesus says they will see “Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the prophets in the kingdom of God.” Those were the big names in the story the listeners already knew. I think the weeping hits harder because those faces are so familiar.

explanations.answer: Moses and Aaron and Miriam and all the priests
explanations.explanation: Moses, Israel's leader, is a great name to have on a list, and you're in good company thinking of him. But this isn't the list Jesus gives. In Luke 13:28 He says the ones thrown out will see “Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the prophets.” The prophets are in there, but the priests aren't.

explanations.answer: David and Solomon and Hezekiah and all the kings
explanations.explanation: David, Israel's king, would be a fine guest at any table, so I see the thinking. But that's not the lineup in verse 28. Jesus says they will see “Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and all the prophets.” He names prophets, and He doesn't mention kings.

All four, baker! Jesus says, “People will come from east and west and north and south…” That's a long guest list. East, west, north and south, and every one of them gets a seat at the table in the kingdom of God.

Judea is a real place, and Jesus had been traveling through towns, so I see why it came to mind. But verse 29 says they come “from east and west and north and south.” That's a lot wider than one region. The table pulls from every direction.

Galilee is a good guess, since Jesus did a lot of His teaching up there. But Luke 13:29 doesn't name a region at all. It says, “People will come from east and west and north and south…” The answer is all four directions.

True. Jesus says, “…some who are last will be first, and some who are first will be last.” That's how He wraps up what He told them about the door and the table. It's a flip, and I think those listeners felt it.
It's actually in there, baker. Jesus says, “…some who are last will be first, and some who are first will be last.” That's verse 30, right after the table. So the answer is True.
True. Some Pharisees come to Jesus and say, “Leave this place and get away, because Herod wants to kill You.” That's a warning with a lot of weight on it. They don't beat around the bush.
The text says it, baker. The Pharisees tell Jesus, “Leave this place and get away, because Herod wants to kill You.” So the answer is True. They said it straight to His face.

explanations.answer: Driving out demons and healing people
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, “…I will keep driving out demons and healing people today and tomorrow…” The warning doesn't change His plans. He just keeps working.

Jesus did teach His disciples, but that's not what He sends to the fox. In Luke 13:32 He says, “…I will keep driving out demons and healing people today and tomorrow…” Nothing in His message is secret. Quiet isn't the plan.

explanations.answer: Staying out of sight in the villages
explanations.explanation: I can see why hiding sounds like a reaction to a threat. But Jesus doesn't say that. His message is, “…I will keep driving out demons and healing people today and tomorrow…” That's work done out in the open.

That one tempts people, since staying put sounds like the careful thing. But Jesus says the opposite. In verse 33 He says, “Nevertheless, I must keep going today and tomorrow and the next day…” He keeps moving.
False, baker. Jesus says, “Nevertheless, I must keep going today and tomorrow and the next day…” He isn't waiting for the danger to pass. He keeps moving toward Jerusalem.

explanations.answer: A hen gathering her chicks under her wings
explanations.explanation: Yes! Jesus says He has longed to gather Jerusalem's children together “as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings.” It's a picture of a mother bird pulling her little ones in close. I think there's real tenderness in that.

explanations.answer: A shepherd gathering his sheep into the fold
explanations.explanation: A shepherd is a picture Jesus uses in other places, so I get why it came to mind. But in Luke 13:34 the picture is different. He says it's “as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings.” This time it's a hen.

explanations.answer: A fisherman gathering his nets into the boat
explanations.explanation: Nets and boats are all over the Gospels, so that's a natural guess. But it's not the picture here. Jesus says He longed to gather them “as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings.” It's a hen and her chicks, not fishing gear.
It's the other way around, baker. Jesus says He longed to gather them, “but you were unwilling!” So the text says Jerusalem was unwilling. That's what makes the line sting.
False, and Jesus says it Himself. He says how often He longed to gather them, “but you were unwilling!” He wanted to gather them, and they weren't willing. I hear sorrow in that.

explanations.answer: Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says, “…you will not see Me again until you say, ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.’” It's a line about welcoming Him. He ends on that note, and so does the passage.

explanations.answer: Truly this was the Son of God
explanations.explanation: Those words are in the Bible, but they come from somewhere else. The centurion guarding Jesus said them at the cross (Matthew 27:54). In Luke 13:35 Jesus names a different line: “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.”

explanations.answer: We have no king but Caesar
explanations.explanation: That line is in the Bible too, but it's from a different moment. The chief priests said it in John 19:15. What Jesus says Jerusalem will say in Luke 13:35 is the opposite kind of line: “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.”
